_about: The changelog's written highlights, one entry per day that shipped. Written from that day's commits (git log), in plain words; the commit list itself is added by scripts/changelog.mjs. `teachers` shows on the console's /changelog; `students` (under `studentTitle`, in a student's words) on the student app's What's new, and only student-facing changes go there. An empty `students` list keeps the day off the student page. Instructor, 7 Oct 2026 (night): both written highlights and the full commit list.

updates.title: Course Studio
teachers: Course Studio replaces Content: one page for the course's material, in the Course group of the menu. One sidebar on the right holds the Outline (subjects, their books and chapters) and the AI Assistant as two tabs.

A chapter is now a page you type on, like a word processor: click into any topic and type, with bold, italic, code, headings and lists on a toolbar above it. Add, delete and reorder topics; quotes from the book and figures stay locked, so the book's words cannot be typed over. A Student view button shows the page as a student reads it. Old Content links still land.

What you type is a draft: it saves itself, and students read none of it until you press Publish, give a reason and see what changes. Discard throws a draft away. The old save-a-block that reached students at once is gone, which answers the question about a second teacher on block edits. Chapters you publish are exported to files for git with pnpm content:export, because the free database keeps no backups
To review gathers summaries, drafted lesson text and figures in one place.
Every teacher can add a subject, rename it, and add, edit or default its books, each with a reason in the audit log.

A new approval rule, held in the database: a teacher of the subject approves, never the author of the version; the admin may approve their own edit, recorded as self-approved. An Approve you may not use is disabled, with the reason beside it.
The AI Assistant pane is there, locked, and says the app is not released yet.

Moons are an editor now. On a chapter, each moon is a row you can edit (its sentence, its ring, its kind of skill), retire, or add to: a new moon is a draft that students never see and that does not hold the next planet shut until it has three live questions.

Typing a change to a moon changes nothing for students. One dialog, Review moon changes, publishes them and says first what will happen: what moves on the map, which minigame leaves it, and how many students would see a planet close until they master a new moon. It asks you for a reason.

Retiring a moon takes it off the map and out of what opens a planet, and keeps every question and every student's record of it. The last moon of a chapter, or one a stage check needs to fill, cannot be retired.
A moon you have edited or added is yours: syncing the chapter files no longer rewords it or brings a retired one back, and the export now writes moons too.
A topic's History is back in the editor: the clock button lists its earlier versions and Use this text puts one back as a draft.

Profile pictures, first half: the database and the server are done and on the live project. A picture is cropped to a square and re-encoded to a small WebP in the student's browser (a phone photo's location data is dropped), stored in a private bucket, and shown to classmates and teachers. A teacher can remove a student's picture, the admin anyone's, each with a reason in the audit log, and the student is told. The roster, a student's record and the teachers list already carry the picture; their pages for it, and your own profile page, are next.

The student chat is Messenger-shaped on a phone: the rooms are a list, and opening a room fills the screen with the room's name, the messages and the composer, with the top bar, tabs and mission panel out of the way. The console's chat is unchanged.
Students get a ? button in the top bar that runs a nine-step tour of the app, and runs by itself once, on their first visit to the map.
students: You can add a profile picture. Choose one, drag it into place, zoom, and use it: your classmates and your teachers see it, and your teacher can remove it. Until you add one, your system draws a planet for you from your student ID. Your name, student number and classes are on the same page, which you reach from your picture in the top bar.

Chat looks and works like Messenger on a phone: the rooms are a list, and opening one fills the screen with the messages, with the bar, tabs and mission panel out of the way. The arrow (or your phone's Back) returns to the rooms. Messages are bubbles with a face beside each speaker.
There is a ? in the top bar. It walks you through the app in nine short steps, and it starts by itself the first time you open the map. Press it whenever you want it again.
